note: Track sevenths-up (theory-building-chords), step 7: the four 7th chords and the two triads, as six chords on G, then named by ear, then the four 7th chords on G in a band. Missing: interval-ears "kind": "chord" has no half-diminished answer, so that chord is heard in the chord boxes and the band only.

exercise.title: Four 7th chords and two triads
exercise.why: Each of the four 7th chords is a triad with a 7th on top, so hearing the three notes underneath first and the top note second tells them from the triads and from each other.

cells.text:
Press a chord box below to hear the chord. Press G and Gm, the two triads, then Gmaj7 and G7: the major triad with a 7th on top, a half step or a whole step under the octave.
Then press Gm7 and Gm7♭5: the minor triad with the lower 7th, and the same chord with its 5th lowered a half step.
Go round the six until you can name each with your eyes closed.

Press Start in the game below: it plays a chord from any root, and you pick Major, Minor, Dominant 7, Major 7 or Minor 7 (Dominant 7 is the chord written 7, as in G7).
Listen to the three notes underneath first, major or minor, then for a 7th on top.
The game does not ask the half-diminished chord: the band in the next block plays it.

Press Play below to start the band: the four 7th chords on G, a bar each, in two orders. Look away from the chord boxes and call out the chord on each change, then look to check.
Listen for the bar where the 5th drops: that is Gm7♭5, the half-diminished chord.
